note: Researched recommendations, written in the site's voice but by somebody who has not been. Opinionated on purpose — a list of facts is not a guide — but every card says plainly that it was researched rather than visited, and a handwritten note in notes.json overrules any of it. This file exists because nothing else can fill it: no open dataset in India describes everyday food, Wikidata holds two Delhi restaurants and no cafes, and the whole sourced tier here is monuments. See SOURCES.md.
rules: Every record needs a source and a lastVerified date. If it cannot be checked, it does not go in.
Say what to order and when to go. 'Lovely atmosphere' helps nobody.
No opening hours in prose. OpenStreetMap carries them, js/hours.js reads them, and a time written here is a time that rots.
quality and uniqueness cap at 4 here. 5 is reserved for somewhere one of you actually loved.
Where a claim is disputed, say it is disputed. Delhi has more than one restaurant claiming to have invented the same dish and at least one of those arguments is in court.

Always pin `match` with a zone. Matching on name alone resolved 'Bukhara' to a restaurant in Noida rather than the one in Chanakyapuri — and the famous one is not in OpenStreetMap at all, so the record was dropped. That is the index doing its job: it is what stops a writer inventing a place.

items.title: Karim's
items.why: In Gali Kababian behind the Jama Masjid since 1913, opened by Haji Karimuddin, whose father cooked in the Mughal court. It began as two dishes — aloo gosht and daal with rumali roti — and those are still the honest order, along with the mutton korma and the seekh kebabs. The nihari is a morning thing and goes early.
items.source: Wikipedia; Slurrp; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Moti Mahal
items.why: Opened in Daryaganj in 1947 by three men who came from Peshawar at Partition, and the place that brought the tandoor to Delhi restaurants — tandoori chicken, dal makhani, butter chicken. Who exactly invented the butter chicken is genuinely disputed and has been in court since 2024, the rival claim coming from the Jaggi family's own restaurant. Go for the tandoori chicken, which nobody argues about.
items.source: Wikipedia; The National; Al Jazeera (2024, on the dispute); existence confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Indian Accent
items.why: The tasting menu that made modern Indian cooking respectable to Indians rather than only to visitors. The blue cheese naan is the dish people describe afterwards. Book weeks out; this is the special-occasion end of the city.
items.source: Wikidata (restaurant in New Delhi); published coverage; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Saravana Bhavan
items.why: South Indian, vegetarian, fast and cheap, and the counter-argument to the idea that Delhi is only Mughlai. Ghee roast dosa and filter coffee. Connaught Place at lunch is the busiest it gets, which is also when it is best.
items.source: Published coverage; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Kake Da Hotel
items.why: Connaught Place since 1931 and not a hotel — a dhaba with a queue. Mutton is what it does; the keema and the butter chicken are the other two orders. Crowded, loud, quick, and cheap for what it is.
items.source: Published coverage; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Lodhi Gardens
items.why: Ninety acres with eleven monuments standing in it — the tombs of Muhammad Shah Sayyid (1444) and Sikandar Lodi, the Bada Gumbad, the Shish Gumbad — laid out as a garden around them in 1936. Delhi walks here in the morning. The octagonal Sayyid tomb is the one to look at properly: Hindu features built into an Indo-Islamic building.
items.source: Wikipedia; Incredible India; position confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Sunder Nursery
items.why: Ninety acres next to Humayun's Tomb, derelict for decades and reopened in 2018 after a ten-year restoration by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture — the charbagh canals rebuilt, the axis to the tomb restored, hundreds of native species planted as Delhi's first arboretum. Six World Heritage monuments stand inside it. Time put it on its list of the world's hundred greatest places that year.
items.source: Wikipedia; Aga Khan Development Network; Delhi Tourism; position confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Agrasen ki Baoli
items.why: A stepwell 60 metres long and 108 steps deep, three storeys of arched niches going down into the ground, and it sits in a lane off Hailey Road with office towers on every side. Attributed by legend to King Agrasen and rebuilt in the fourteenth century by the Agarwal community. ASI-protected, free, and almost nobody there on a weekday morning.
items.source: Archaeological Survey of India listing; India Heritage; position confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Bahrisons Booksellers
items.why: Khan Market, since 1953, opened by Balraj Bahri Malhotra — nineteen when he came from Malakwal at Partition, and he raised the capital by selling one of his mother's gold bangles. Seventy years of stocking the same families. Still independent, still the best general bookshop in the city.
items.source: Wikipedia; The Better India; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Blue Tokai Coffee Roasters
items.why: The roaster that started Indians drinking Indian coffee as something other than instant — single-estate beans from Karnataka and Kerala, roasted here, and the reason a specialty scene exists in this city at all. Ask what is fresh off the roaster rather than ordering from the board.
items.source: Published coverage; existence confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Bengali Sweet House
items.why: Bengali Market, and despite the name the thing to have is the chaat — the raj kachori, the gol gappe — with the mithai afterwards rather than instead. Cheap, standing room, and it has been the same for decades.
items.source: Published coverage; existence and address confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Khari Baoli Spice Market
items.why: Asia's largest wholesale spice market, trading on this street since the seventeenth century, at the western end of Chandni Chowk beside the Fatehpuri Masjid that Shah Jahan's wife built in 1650. The name means salty stepwell, after the baoli travellers once watered animals at. Go early, breathe shallowly for the first ten minutes, and buy whole spices by weight rather than ground.
items.source: Wikipedia; Craftsmanship Magazine; Media India; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Lajpat Nagar Central Market
items.why: South Delhi's loudest market, and it exists because of Partition — Lajpat Nagar was laid out in 1950 for Punjabi refugees who arrived with nothing, and the market is what they built. Clothes, fabric, shoes and household things at prices worth the crush. Evenings are busiest; the mehndi stalls at the Central Market end are the thing people come back for.
items.source: Wikipedia; Delhi Tourism; The Patriot; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Nai Sarak Bookshop Area
items.why: A street the British cut through Old Delhi after 1857 — officially Egerton Road, and nobody has ever called it that — lined with early twentieth-century buildings whose ground floors are all booksellers. Wholesale textbooks mostly, shop by shop specialising: medical here, children's there, one for languages. Trade has fallen hard this decade, which is a reason to go now rather than later.
items.source: Wikipedia; published coverage; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Meena Bazaar
items.why: The lanes under the Jama Masjid's eastern steps, selling prayer caps, attar, kebabs and hardware in roughly that order of density. It is a market to walk rather than to shop — go after visiting the mosque, in the late afternoon, and eat on the way out.
items.source: Published coverage; position confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Wenger's
items.why: The oldest surviving establishment in Connaught Place. A Swiss couple, Jeanne and H C Wenger, started it in 1926 at Kashmere Gate catering for British troops, and moved it into the Robert Tor Russell building in 1933 — with a café and a ballroom that officers, diplomats and princes filled. Brij Mohan Tandon, who had worked for them, bought it in 1944. Buy the patties and a slice of something from the cold counter and eat in the colonnade.
items.source: ThePrint; Slurrp; Delhipedia; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: L'Opera
items.why: The patisserie that brought French pastry to India when it opened in 2008, and still the reference for it here. Khan Market, next door to Full Circle. The macarons are why people come; the croissant is why they come back.
items.source: the bakery's own history; Tripadvisor listing; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Cafe Lota
items.why: Inside the National Crafts Museum, opposite Purana Qila, in a half-open room built by the craftsmen the museum exists for. Regional Indian cooking you will not find on a Delhi menu elsewhere, and South Indian filter coffee. Do the museum, then lunch; it is the right order.
items.source: National Crafts Museum; Atlas Obscura; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Kunzum Travel Cafe
items.why: In the lanes of Hauz Khas Village, and the coffee and the cookies come with no price on them — you pay what you think they were worth. Travel books to read, travel talks and screenings in the evenings. Shut on Mondays.
items.source: Tripadvisor listing; LBB; Let's Expresso; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Subko Cafe
items.why: The Mumbai roastery and bakehouse that opened in a restored Bandra bungalow in 2020, and this is its Delhi outpost in Lodhi Colony's Khanna Market. Order from the coffee menu rather than the milk menu, and a pastry from the counter — the bakehouse is half the point.
items.source: Subko; The Gourmet Edit; New Delhi Wants; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Blue Tokai Coffee Roasters
items.why: The Chittaranjan Park branch of the roaster on the Lodhi Colony card — single-estate beans from Karnataka and Kerala, roasted in-house. Here for the south-east of the city, which otherwise has almost nothing on record for coffee.
items.source: Published coverage; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Indian Coffee House
items.why: A workers' cooperative since 1957, when Nehru told the coffee-house workers to run the places themselves. Thrown out of its first building during the Emergency, it reopened on the roof of Mohan Singh Place, where it still is — waiters in turbans and cummerbunds, dosa and filter coffee at prices from another decade, and a room that has hosted every political argument Delhi has had since.
items.source: Wikipedia; Cambridge University Press (ILWCH, 2026); Slurrp; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Bahrisons Booksellers
items.why: The Saket branch of the Khan Market bookshop on the card in Lodhi Colony — the one Balraj Bahri Malhotra opened in 1953 with the price of his mother's gold bangle. Here for the south of the city, which otherwise reaches all the way to Khan Market for a bookshop.
items.source: Wikipedia; LBB; Outlook Traveller; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Roasters Coffee Co. Book Cafe
items.why: A café Bahrisons opened inside its own shop, so the books are the room. Buy something, sit down with it and a coffee; it is one of the few places in south Delhi built for exactly that.
items.source: Thoughts by Geethica; Outlook Traveller; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Suchali's Artisan Bakehouse
items.why: Sourdough, bagels and proper European loaves. Suchali Jain, from finance, and Mitali Singh started it in 2018 on twenty lakh of their own money after Suchali had eaten her way round European bakeries. This is the Dwarka shop, which gives the far south-west something other than a chain to buy bread from.
items.source: YourStory; the bakery's own site; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Suchali's Artisan Bakehouse
items.why: The same sourdough bakery as the Dwarka card, in the NCR sectors — which is where this guide otherwise has almost nothing but chains. Suchali's began in Gurugram before it came into Delhi.
items.source: YourStory; the bakery's own site; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Sibang Bakery
items.why: A Korean-owned bakery in South Point Mall on Golf Course Road, and the reason people from the rest of Gurgaon drive to a mall on purpose. Soft Korean breads and cream buns rather than anything French, which is the point of it.
items.source: LBB; Tripadvisor listing; confirmed against OpenStreetMap

items.title: Another Fine Day

match.name: Another Fine Day Cafe and Reading Room

items.why: A café and reading room on Golf Course Road that opens at eight and serves breakfast all day — somewhere in Gurgaon that is not trying to be a mall, while standing next to several. Bring a book or borrow one.
items.source: LBB; the café's own site; confirmed against OpenStreetMap
